description: Requests a user of a coding agent types (English and Vietnamese), each with the skills a person would expect the product to select for it. Used by tests/tools/measure-skill-selection.mjs and tests/verify-skill-selection-baseline.mjs to measure the keyword selector (PluginManager.selectSkillsForTask and selectConversationSkills) as it is. The labels were written from the skills' names and descriptions alone, before the selector was run on any row; the commit that adds this file is older than the commit that adds the first results.

fresh.note: The three skills a first start installs and enables (installedByDefault in MARKETPLACE_CATALOG).

shipped.note: All nine skills of MARKETPLACE_CATALOG, enabled.

large.note: The nine shipped skills and the thirty stand-in third-party skills of skill-selection-third-party.json, installed after them in the order of that file.

projectKinds.note: A row's `project` lists the kinds of project its workspace is. The measuring script makes a temporary folder with these files and lets the real detectProjectSignals read it.

labelling: Every row is judged against ONE set of enabled skills (`set`). `must`: the skills a person who turned these skills on would expect to be given for the request; an entry that is a list means any one of those is enough (two skills that do the same job). `acceptable`: skills whose selection is not a mistake and is not required. `mustNot`: skills that the wording could tempt a word matcher into and that are plainly wrong here. A selected skill that is in neither `must` nor `acceptable` counts as over-selection, whether or not it is listed in `mustNot`.

A skill is expected when the request asks for WORK the description says the skill guides, not when it merely contains a word of it. Writing a commit message, naming a branch or opening a pull request expects git-workflow-pro (its description names exactly those three); other git operations (rebase, merge, log) only make it acceptable.

Naming a technology in a QUESTION ("explain what git rebase does", "what is Docker?") expects nothing: these skills are guidance for doing work, and an explanation does not need them. The skill of that technology is `acceptable` there (carrying it is a cost, not an error). Naming a technology in passing while asking for other work, or using a word of a skill in another sense ("branch coverage", "worker pool", "commits the transaction"), puts that skill in `mustNot`.

A request with no sign of the language or the kind of project ("write tests for this function") expects nothing; where one skill is the likely one it is `acceptable`. With a `project` the kind is known: changing or testing code in a Python project expects python-architect, building user interface in a React project expects the React skill, and so on, while a request that has nothing to do with the kind (a typo in the README) still expects nothing.

A follow-up (`earlier` holds the conversation's previous requests, oldest first) expects the skills of the work it continues. When it changes the subject, only the new subject's skills are expected and the earlier ones are `acceptable`.

Handling credentials, tokens, private keys or licences of dependencies expects security-compliance-guard, also when the request does not say "security". In the large set an explicit security REVIEW of code expects openai-security-best-practices, with the guard acceptable.
Chit-chat and questions about the product itself expect nothing.

`lang`: en; vi (Vietnamese with diacritics); vi-plain (Vietnamese typed without diacritics); mixed (Vietnamese and English in one request). `category`: one (exactly one skill clearly helps), two (two help), none (nothing should be selected: general coding, chit-chat, the product), followup (a turn that only makes sense with the earlier ones), mention (a technology or a skill's word is named and the skill is not wanted), project (the request does not name the technology; the workspace shows it).
